definition: The set of assumptions a learning algorithm uses to make predictions on inputs it hasn't specifically seen before.
details: Inductive bias is built into model architecture choices — for example, convolutional networks assume spatial locality matters, while transformers make comparatively fewer built-in assumptions about input structure, relying more on data to learn such patterns.
story: Picture guardrails on a mountain road — not there to slow you down on the straightaways, but to keep you from flying off the cliff. It is the habit of asking, before every launch, what could go wrong — and then doing something about it. Think of it as the quiet rule that a tool should be useful without being dangerous. It is the difference between “it works” and “it is safe to put in front of people.” That deliberate caution is Inductive Bias.
